titre: In 1918, German Industrialists Recognize Unions by Contract
accroche: Berlin, November 15, 1918: six days after the revolution reaches Berlin, employers and unions sign union recognition and the eight-hour day.
contenu_vulgarise:
Berlin, November 15, 1918. Six days after November 9, when revolution broke out in the capital, employers' federations and the free, Christian, and Polish trade unions sign a thirteen-point text. On the employers' side are the Ruhr industrialist Hugo Stinnes, Walther Rathenau for AEG, Carl Friedrich von Siemens, and Alfred Hugenberg; on the union side, Carl Legien, president of the General Commission of German Trade Unions, and Adam Stegerwald for the Christian unions. The text keeps the first two names: the Stinnes-Legien Agreement.

## What the Employers Concede

Point 1 recognizes all trade unions as the legitimate representation of workers. Point 2 declares any restriction of freedom of association inadmissible. Point 3 commits employers to leaving the "Werkvereine" (so-called peaceful company associations) to fend for themselves from now on, without supporting them directly or indirectly.

Point 6 provides that working conditions be set by collective agreements with workers' organizations, to be negotiated without delay. Point 7 creates a workers' committee in every establishment with at least fifty employees. Point 9 caps the working day at eight hours, with no loss of pay. A joint central committee is tasked with applying the whole: its decisions bind both sides, unless an organization appeals within a week (points 10 to 12).

## A Concession Born of Fear

Nothing in this list looks like a conversion. The German Wikipedia article on the agreement reports that the industrialists, a few days into the revolution, feared the socialization of their factories, and quotes the historian Arthur Rosenberg: they were ready for anything, as long as they kept their property.

The state, for its part, had already taken a step two years earlier. The German Auxiliary Service Law of December 5, 1916, had recognized unions as legitimate representatives of workers. In 1918, it is the employers themselves who take the step, through a private contract. On November 12, the Council of People's Deputies, the government that emerged from the revolution, had promised the eight-hour day for January 1, 1919 (Wikipedia); the agreement establishes it from the moment of signing.

## A Contract Waiting for Its Law

The last point is the most telling. The agreement takes effect on the day of signing and holds "vorbehaltlich anderweitiger gesetzlicher Regelung" (subject to other statutory regulation), until further notice, with three months' mutual notice. It thus presents itself as valid until further notice and subject to a law.

That is what happens. On December 23, 1918, a German ordinance on collective agreements, workers' and employees' committees, and the settlement of labor disputes (Reichsgesetzblatt 1918, p. 1456) draws on it for collective agreements and committees, the agreement having served as its model according to Wikipedia. The Collective Agreements Act of April 9, 1949, adopted for the unified economic zone of western Germany, will extend this lineage.

The general recognition of unions as bargaining partners therefore does not arise from a law passed to protect employees, but from a contract drafted under the threat of socialization, which the law then took up. What remains to be seen is what a right granted out of fear is worth once the fear has faded.

repere.texte: Point 9 of the November 15, 1918 agreement: the maximum daily working time is set at eight hours for all establishments, with no reduction in pay because of this shortening ("Verdienstschmälerungen aus Anlaß dieser Verkürzung der Arbeitszeit dürfen nicht stattfinden", i.e. "no loss of earnings on account of this shortening of working hours may take place").

carte.punch: In 1918, German employers recognize unions by contract; the law follows afterward.
carte.idee: On November 15, 1918, German employers and unions sign thirteen points: unions recognized, collective agreements, the eight-hour day. The industrialists feared the socialization of their factories. An ordinance of December 23, 1918 draws on the agreement.

quiz.question: What fear pushes German industrialists to sign the Stinnes-Legien Agreement in November 1918?
choix: A general strike by railway workers that would paralyze the soldiers' return
A decision by the new government to nationalize the Ruhr mines
The socialization of their factories in the midst of revolution
Competition from neighboring countries that already had the eight-hour day
quiz.explication: The Wikipedia article quotes Arthur Rosenberg: the great industrialists feared socialization and wanted to keep their property. The text of the agreement mentions neither a railway strike, nor a nationalization decided by the government, nor foreign competition: it is a private contract, signed out of fear of socialization.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does point 9 of the Stinnes-Legien Agreement set?
choix: An identical minimum wage in all sectors
A working day of eight hours maximum, with no loss of pay
A forty-hour week, paid as overtime
One additional day off per month for all employees
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Point 9 caps the working day at eight hours, with no reduction in pay because of this shortening. The agreement sets neither a minimum wage, nor a forty-hour week, nor an additional day off.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does point 7 of the agreement create, in every establishment with at least fifty employees?
choix: A workers' committee for the establishment
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Point 7 creates a workers' committee in every establishment with at least fifty employees. The agreement provides for no pension fund and no arbitration court, and point 3 on the contrary commits employers to leaving company associations to fend for themselves.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens on December 23, 1918, a month after the agreement is signed?
choix: The revolutionary government denounces the agreement as insufficient
The industrialists obtain the cancellation of point 9 on the eight-hour day
A German ordinance on collective agreements and committees draws on the agreement
The Treaty of Versailles takes up the text's thirteen points
quiz_supplementaire.explication: A German ordinance on collective agreements, workers' and employees' committees, and the settlement of labor disputes draws on the agreement, according to Wikipedia. No denunciation, cancellation, or takeover by a treaty is mentioned.
